what_it_does: When a compiler translates your source code into machine instructions, it also emits a separate table of debugging information — a map that lets a debugger (like GDB) show you which line of source code is executing and what your variables currently hold. Bugs in that debugging information mean the debugger shows you wrong values or wrong locations, making software development much harder. The existing way to test for such bugs is to compare program behavior between an optimized and an unoptimized build, but optimized code rearranges instructions so heavily that the comparison breaks down. Cross-Level Debugging (CLD) sidesteps this by running the very same executable twice under the same debugger — once viewed at the source-code level and once at the raw machine-instruction level — and checking that both views tell a consistent story about where the program is and what it holds. Any discrepancy flags a bug in the debugger toolchain. This is from the abstract only.
